title: Bookstore Inventory & Cart
description: Implement optimistic locking for inventory management, cart expiration strategies, session management for guest and authenticated users, and wishlist functionality.

segments.text: Two customers see the last copy of a popular book. Both add it to their cart. Both click checkout. Without proper concurrency control, you oversell — fulfillment fails, customers are angry, and your reviews suffer. Amazon handles this with optimistic locking on inventory, checking stock at the moment of purchase, not when the item was added to cart.

Optimistic locking: read the inventory record with its version number. When decrementing stock, include a WHERE version equals the_read_version clause. If another transaction updated the stock first, the version changed, the update affects zero rows, and you know to retry or reject. No locks held during the customer's browsing time.

Cart data model: cart_id, user_id (nullable for guests), items array with book_id and quantity, created_at, and updated_at. Store carts in Redis for speed with periodic persistence to the database. Guest carts use a session cookie for identification. On login, merge the guest cart with the user's existing cart — handle quantity conflicts by taking the maximum.

Cart expiration prevents inventory hoarding. If a user adds items but doesn't checkout within two hours, release the items back to available inventory. But don't delete the cart — keep it for seven days so returning users find their selections. Implement with a TTL on the inventory reservation, separate from the cart lifetime.

A flash sale starts. One thousand users add the same book to their carts in ten seconds. You have fifty copies. Do you reserve inventory when added to cart, or check at checkout? Each approach has tradeoffs.
segments.thought_prompt: Reserve inventory on add-to-cart (better UX) vs check-at-checkout (higher conversion)? Justify your choice.

segments.text: Session management for guest users: generate a UUID session token, store in an HTTP-only secure cookie. Map session to cart in Redis. For authenticated users, store the user ID in a JWT. Session hijacking prevention: rotate session tokens on login, bind sessions to IP ranges, and set short session timeouts for sensitive operations like checkout.

Wishlists are simpler than carts — no inventory reservation, no expiration. Data model: user_id, book_id, added_at. Support 'move to cart' which adds to cart and removes from wishlist atomically. Wishlists also drive notifications: alert users when wishlist items go on sale or are back in stock. This is a key re-engagement feature.

Price consistency is tricky. The user sees a price on the product page, adds to cart, but by checkout the price has changed. Do you honor the displayed price or the current price? Amazon's approach: show the current price in the cart and notify the user of changes. Never charge more than the displayed price without explicit confirmation.

Cart persistence strategy: write-through to Redis on every cart update for fast access. Async persist to PostgreSQL every thirty seconds for durability. If Redis fails, fall back to database reads — slower but data is preserved. Cart recovery on Redis cold start: load active carts from the database into Redis during startup.

Design the inventory and cart system for a bookstore handling Black Friday: fifty thousand concurrent users, five hundred checkouts per minute, and one thousand unique titles with varying stock levels. What's your complete architecture?
segments.thought_prompt: Design inventory + cart for Black Friday: 50K concurrent users, 500 checkouts/min.

segments.text: Bookstore inventory uses optimistic locking to prevent overselling, Redis-backed carts with database persistence for speed and durability, timed inventory reservations to prevent hoarding, and session-based guest cart management with merge-on-login. The key insight: separate the cart lifecycle from the inventory reservation lifecycle.
